crops.description_beginner: The easiest tomato to start with, and there's a specific reason why. Most cherry tomatoes are indeterminate, meaning the plant keeps producing new flower clusters and fruit continuously from early summer until frost, instead of ripening everything at once and stopping. One plant can give you handfuls of tomatoes over 10-14 weeks. That same continuous growth habit also means the plant recovers better from uneven watering or a missed feeding than a tomato that puts everything into one big harvest. Modern hybrid varieties like Sun Gold and Sweet 100 also have built-in disease resistance, which lowers the chances of losing a plant to blight. If you're in a cold zone (3-5), look for short-season varieties labeled under 60 days to maturity. If you're in a warm zone (9-11), you can get a second round of tomatoes by planting again in late summer. For containers or small spaces, compact varieties like Patio Choice or Tumbling Tom are the right pick.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: One planting gives you tomatoes all summer until frost kills the plant, no need to replant mid-season. If you're in a warm climate like Zone 9 or warmer (think Southern California, Phoenix, or South Florida), you can start a second planting in late summer for a fall and winter harvest.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Not a true succession crop, one planting produces all season. In Zone 9+ you can start a second batch in late summer for a winter harvest.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Produces continuously from one planting all season. In Zone 9+ a second late-summer sowing can extend into winter.

crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick when the tomato is fully colored all the way through, red, yellow, orange, or black depending on what you planted, and gives just slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin shifting from shiny to slightly matte is a reliable visual cue that it's ready. A ripe tomato should twist off easily; if you have to pull hard, give it one more day. Try to harvest in the morning when it's cooler, as tomatoes held in hot sun deteriorate faster.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow cherry tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat: you plant after the last spring frost, pick all summer, and the plants are finished when the first fall frost arrives. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Wait to set out transplants until a week or two after your last frost, when nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. Cherry tomatoes ripen fast (about 55 to 65 days after transplanting), so they finish in time even where summers are short. In the coldest zones, pick quick varieties and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers; in the milder zones 6 and 7 you have time to plant a second batch in early summer for a fall crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows cherry tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Cherry types (55 to 65 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Cherry types are heat resistant, so this pause is shorter for them than for large-fruited tomatoes, and a few varieties keep setting through it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow cherry tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Cherry tomatoes take the heat better than big tomatoes, so their summer break is shorter. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the worst heat, then plant again in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two cherry tomato seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Cherry types handle this better than large-fruited tomatoes: they are heat resistant and quick to mature, so the summer pause is shorter for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Time the spring crop to ripen before peak heat; set the fall crop out in mid-to-late summer to produce into the cooler autumn. The warmer zone 9 end of the region plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant cherry tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here cherry tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow cherry tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Cherry types are heat resistant and keep setting fruit through the peak valley heat better than large-fruited tomatoes, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop here. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set cherry tomato transplants out along the North Coast in May, once the marine-influenced spring has warmed enough for the plants to grow. The limiting factor here is heat, not frost: the last frost passes earlier, but tomatoes wait for warmth because coastal nights can sit below 55 degrees F in any month and cool summers slow growth. In Marin and similar coastal counties early May is usually warm enough to transplant. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

harvest_end.source_quote: North & North Coast: May

The season is bounded on the back end by falling temperatures and light rather than by a hard frost: coastal first frost comes late, but cherry production winds down once the warm-season window closes. Microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm locally. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's North Coast (the foggy coast from about Monterey north, including Marin), you plant cherry tomatoes once, in May, and then pick them through summer into early fall. Here the thing holding tomatoes back is a lack of heat, not frost: the coast stays cool and foggy, and nights can drop below 55°F even in summer, so the plants need the warmer late-spring weather before they will really grow. Wait until May to set out transplants, give them the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have, and choose varieties that do well in cool summers. There is no second fall planting here, because the warm season is short.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows cherry tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives North & North Coast tomatoes as May (transplant), a single month with no semicolon and no fall window (contrast the table's genuine two-window crops such as snap beans 'July; May-June'). UC Marin Master Gardeners ('Tomato time!') independently confirms an early-May transplant and the cool-limit mechanism (Marin nights below 55F in any month; tomatoes need warmth). The warm season is SHORT because summer never gets hot enough (marine layer, sub-55F nights), NOT because of a midsummer heat exclusion. No heat_pause is authored: there is no summer pause, the season is bounded by lack of heat at both shoulders. Contrast ca_desert / ca_interior summer behavior.

Coastal zone 9b/10a first frost is late (Nov-Dec or later), but cherry production winds down in October as the warm-season window closes. harvest_end set to end of October; calendar fall months read 'wait' rather than 'cold_pause' because the season closes on heat/light, not frost. Table 13.2's own disclaimer (microclimate varies sharply) is surfaced in region_notes.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's South Coast (the mild coast of San Diego and the Los Angeles basin), you plant cherry tomatoes once, anytime from April through about mid-July, and then pick them through summer and fall. Right on the frost-free coast you can often harvest all the way to the end of the year. The weather here is gentle, so there is no summer break in planting the way hotter inland and southeastern areas have, and there is no separate fall crop, just one long season from a single planting. Plant when the soil has warmed and give the plants full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows cherry tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cherry types are heat resistant and set well through the warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

This is the inverse of cold-climate timing: in Imperial and Coachella the winter is the growing season and the summer is the exclusion. heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant cherry types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella), the calendar is flipped: you grow cherry tomatoes in the cool months and take the summer off, because summer here is too hot for tomatoes to make fruit. Plant your main crop in winter, from December through mid-March, so the plants can grow and set fruit before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (often over 110°F), and tomato flowers will not set, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through the mild late fall and winter. Even heat-loving cherry tomatoes cannot handle the peak desert summer, so the summer break is not optional here.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow cherry tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance: unlike the milder southeastern Gulf summer, desert peak heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant cherry types. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives Desert Valleys tomatoes as 'Dec-March' -- the mild-winter MAIN plant window (inverted calendar). UC Statewide IPM Program and UC ANR home-garden guidance anchor the summer heat-exclusion mechanism (desert summer daytime highs past 95-110F; fruit set fails above ~95F as viable pollen collapses). The two-window structure (winter-spring main + September fall crop bracketing a lethal summer) is the canonical desert pattern; UC Riverside County MG (Coachella low desert, read-not-cited, not catalogued) and University of Arizona Extension 'Growing Tomatoes' (low-desert two-season, read-not-cited, AZ source) independently corroborate. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted calendar: winter is the growing season, summer is the exclusion. Main plant window Dec-Mar (mild winter), summer heat_pause Jun-Aug, fall replant Sep. This is the heat-inverted mirror of the cool-limited ca_north_coast and the mild ca_south_coast.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). Climatic-absolute exclusion: Imperial/Coachella peak summer (>95-110F) stops fruit set. Mechanism anchored to UC IPM / UC ANR 8159 (>95F collapses viable pollen).
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_not_narrowed: CONTRAST se_gulf (gs_exemplar_finding_001): there, cherry's heat resistance narrowed the pause to a single month (month 7). HERE the desert pause is NOT narrowed by cherry resistance -- peak desert summer heat is so extreme that even heat-tolerant cherry types cannot set fruit. The Jun-Aug pause is the real lethal span regardless of cherry resistance. This is a per-region cherry judgment, not a universal narrowing.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set cherry tomato transplants out in spring once frost danger has passed. For Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley (zone 8, Chihuahuan high desert) the average last frost is around March 19, so a beginner-safe transplant date is mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart shows an earlier, early-March transplant (seed started indoors in mid-January); that earlier date reflects experienced-grower practice setting plants out right at or just before the frost-free point, often with frost protection. For a first season, waiting until after the last frost is the more reliable choice. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

Cherry types, being heat resistant and quick to set in the cooler arid mornings and evenings, hold a little longer into early summer than large-fruited tomatoes before the brief midsummer pause. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

Cherry and grape varieties suit the fall window well because of their shorter days to maturity. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

The local Las Cruces planting chart shows this second tomato transplant window; it is timed to follow the brief midsummer fruit-set pause. (Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart; NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.source_quote: harvest ... before frost
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to the first fall frost, which in Las Cruces (zone 8 high desert) arrives around mid-November. Cherry types, heat resistant and quick to mature, make the most of the shorter fall window. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the warm arid Southwest, daytime temperatures above about 95°F at the peak of midsummer push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail (NMSU Circular 457 gives 95°F day and 55°F night as the set thresholds). Cherry types are heat resistant and the arid climate's cool nights aid recovery, so this pause is brief, roughly the single hottest month, and shorter for cherry than for large-fruited tomatoes. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Where you live gets very hot in midsummer, so cherry tomatoes grow best in two rounds. Plant the first round in mid to late March, after the last frost, and you will start picking tomatoes in mid to late May. When it gets hottest, around July, the plants stop setting new tomatoes for a few weeks because the flowers cannot set in the heat. Plant a second round in mid to late July for a fall crop that keeps going into November, until the first frost. Cherry tomatoes handle heat well and your cool nights help, so they bounce back faster than big tomatoes.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid Southwest, including Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley in zone 8, gives cherry tomatoes two planting windows around the peak of summer heat. Set the first crop out in mid to late March, once frost danger has passed (the average last frost is around March 19), for a harvest that begins in mid to late May, well before the most intense heat arrives. Through the hottest stretch of midsummer, daytime temperatures above about 95°F suppress fruit set, so production lulls for roughly the single hottest month, around July. Set a second crop out in mid to late July, transplanting through the heat so plants establish and then set as temperatures ease, for a fall harvest that runs into early November until the first frost. Cherry varieties handle the heat better than large slicing tomatoes and the cool desert nights help them keep setting, so the summer lull is shorter for them. A note on sourcing: the spring window follows NMSU statewide guidance and Las Cruces frost data, while the second, midsummer planting comes from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces planting chart, a single regional Master Gardener source that we have not been able to corroborate independently. The Dona Ana chart also shows an earlier, early-March transplant for the spring crop, which reflects experienced-grower practice setting out right at the frost-free point; a mid-to-late-March transplant is the more reliable first-season choice.

plantings_provenance.structure_basis: Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart shows two distinct tomato transplant windows (Path A chart read 2026-06-07: 1st transplant early March, 2nd transplant mid-July) separated by a midsummer set-failure window; NMSU Circular 457 fruit-set thresholds (>95F day) plus Mesilla Valley high-desert summer climate independently support a midsummer set-failure pause at month 7. Spring dates frost-anchored (arid_highland); fall dates single-source (MG chart, uncorroborated, disclosed).
plantings_provenance.spring_date_basis: Spring transplant timed to the zone-8 arid_highland last frost (Mar 19; Chihuahuan high desert, BSk; confirmed against NOAA 30% last-32F for Las Cruces = Mar 20). Beginner-safe plant-out mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County MG chart's earlier early-March transplant (seed mid-Jan) is the seasoned/source anchor, reflecting experienced-grower practice at/just before frost-free. Beginner-safety divergence (hybrid ruling, same pattern as low_desert_az). CORRECTS the prior desert-analogy May transplant.
plantings_provenance.fall_window_basis: Fall transplant window (mid-to-late July; start indoors mid-June) taken from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart (Path A chart read, 2026-06-07: tomato row shows 1st planting start mid-Jan -> transplant early March; 2nd planting start mid-June -> transplant mid-July). SINGLE-SOURCE, not independently corroborated; disclosed in region_notes_seasoned. Harvest re-derived to arid_highland first frost (Nov 12).

The chart transplants the fall crop IN mid-July, so July is not a do-not-plant month; it is the peak fruit-set-failure window (CR457: >95F day stops set). Calendar token at month 7 = heat_pause, mirroring the shipped se_gulf zone-8 cherry cell (same biology: fall transplant into peak-heat July, plant action carried by second_planting{} on its own track). heat_pause.months=[7] kept coherent with calendar[Jul]=heat_pause for release_verify. Mesilla Valley zone 8 is hot but arid with strong nighttime recovery (nights into the 60s), unlike the zone-9 low deserts where the pause is climatic-absolute and not narrowed. Beefsteak re-derives independently and will likely hold a wider pause.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start seeds indoors or in a greenhouse in January, six weeks before the last frost
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the spring crop, start cherry tomato seed indoors in late fall to early winter so transplants are ready by February. The Arizona low desert runs an inverted, race-the-heat calendar: the spring crop must be in the ground early to set fruit before summer. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: start in mid-March in Southern Arizona as soon as frost damage has ended
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the spring cherry tomato crop out in the low desert in February, right after the last frost, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat wall. In Phoenix and the Maricopa low desert that heat wall hits hard by late May, so early planting is essential. Choose short-season cherry or plum types (45 to 80 days). (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop begins ripening about two months after the February transplant, bringing fruit in April and May before the heat shuts production down. Short-season cherry types make the narrow spring window. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Poor fruit development during the heat of summer in southern Arizona (July - August) is expected
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring harvest ends in late May to June as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season in September after the heat passes. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.source_quote: Start new seeds for September planting in June
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed in June (or take cuttings from straggly spring plants in August) so transplants are ready for a September planting. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.source_quote: Gardeners will get a second chance for healthy tomatoes in September, when summer heat has passed
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in September as the summer heat passes. Without the hard deadline the spring crop faces, fall plants have time to grow and produce well into the mild low-desert winter. Many low-desert gardeners consider fall their better tomato season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.source_quote: hit peak production in October and November
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop reaches peak production in October and November, when low-desert weather is mild. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.source_quote: fall plants can grow and produce well into December in the low desert
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest runs into December in the low desert before winter frost ends the season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma, and similar), the calendar is flipped and you get two short tomato seasons around a too-hot summer. Plant your spring crop early, in February right after the last frost, and pick fruit in April and May before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (over 90°F) for tomatoes to set fruit, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through fall and into December, which many desert gardeners think is the better season. Pick fast-maturing cherry types (45 to 80 days) so they finish before the heat. Even heat-loving cherry tomatoes cannot set fruit in peak desert summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Maricopa, Yuma) grows cherry tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar around a hard summer heat exclusion. The spring crop is transplanted early, in February right after the last frost, and must set fruit before the heat wall arrives by late May; it harvests April into June. June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs above 90°F collapse viable pollen), so planting pauses. A fall crop is set out in September once the heat passes and produces through the mild desert fall into December, often the more productive of the two seasons. Short-season cherry and plum types (45 to 80 days) are essential to make the narrow spring window. As in the California desert, the summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078 'Growing Tomatoes' (peer-reviewed, Feb 2024) states the low desert allows two short growing seasons; poor fruit development in the heat of summer (July-August); a second chance in September when summer heat has passed; fall plants produce into December. Maricopa County planting calendar az1005 and the AZ1615 Yuma guide corroborate the spring (Feb) / fall (Sep) two-season structure. Spring transplant Feb (race the late-May heat wall); fall plant Sep. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted two-window calendar like ca_desert, but with AZ-specific dates: spring window opens LATER (February transplant, racing the late-May Phoenix heat wall) than the CA desert's Dec-March winter window; fall replant September into December. Zone 9 only.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). az2078: poor fruit development July-August; >90F reduces viable pollen and stops fruit set.
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_not_narrowed: Same judgment as ca_desert: the desert summer pause is NOT narrowed by cherry's heat resistance (contrast se_gulf month-7 single-month narrowing). Peak low-desert summer heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant cherry types.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_present: Zone 9 two-season. Discrete fall crop: start_indoors Jun, plant_out Sep, harvest_start late Oct, harvest_end mid-Dec. az2078 notes fall is often the better season (no hard heat deadline). Discrete second_planting, not succession.
plantings_provenance.zone_9_only: low_desert_az is zone 9 ONLY per the region_source_map Phase B correction: U of Arizona (Yuma AZ1615) reaches ~10a but is thin there; zone-10 desert is well-served by ca_desert (UC ANR Desert Valleys, Imperial/Coachella). Did not extend low_desert_az to zone 10.

Single-institution sufficient: az2078 is peer-reviewed and az1005 is the county planting calendar, two UofA documents agreeing. No CA or out-of-region source carried (climate-contamination guard).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Start seeds of eggplant, okra, peppers, pumpkin, squashes, and tomatoes for the fall garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the cherry tomato season is the cool, dry half of the year, so seed is started in late summer for fall transplanting. UF/IFAS South Florida starts tomato seed in August for the fall garden; counting back about six weeks from the September-October transplant window places indoor sowing in August. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Easy crops that can be grown now include beans, broccoli, carrots, collards, lettuce, green onions, peppers, radishes, spinach, and tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set cherry tomato transplants out across the long cool-season window. The South Florida calendar opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October and keeps planting open through February, the last month to plant tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Frost is rare on the peninsula, so this is one continuous cross-year window rather than separate spring and fall crops. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cherry tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplant (about 55 to 70 days to maturity). With fall transplanting from September into the fall, the peninsula's cool-season harvest begins in November and carries through the mild winter and spring. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular cherry tomato production runs through the mild winter and spring and winds down as peak-summer heat arrives. Larger-fruited tomatoes stop earlier and are grown as a cool-season crop only; cherry types, being heat resistant, hold a productive tail into early summer before the July-August pause. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; cherry types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists cherry tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; cherry types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists cherry tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula (roughly Orlando south to Miami and the Keys), cherry tomatoes are a cool-weather crop. Frost is rare here, so you plant in the fall, from about September through February, and pick through the mild winter and spring. The hard part is summer, not winter. In July and August it gets too hot, over about 78°F at night, for tomatoes to set fruit, so plants take a break then. Big slicing tomatoes only grow in the cool season here, but cherry types handle the heat better, so they hold on a little into early summer and a few keep going. Pick fast-maturing cherry varieties and start your seeds indoors in August for fall planting.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows cherry tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; cherry types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing cherry types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UF/IFAS divides Florida into North, Central, and South planting regions; the Florida peninsula (zones 10-11) is South Florida, served by one calendar (ENH1191/EP452 South Florida Gardening Calendar) plus VH021's statewide guide. EP452 (rev. Oct 2024) opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October ('tomatoes' listed in the October planting list) and closes the cool-season planting in February ('last month to plant ... tomatoes for a late spring harvest'); August is tomato seed-start for the fall garden. Frost is rare in South Florida (VH021). This is ONE continuous cross-year cool-season window, NOT the desert two-window shape and NOT two discrete crops -> no second_planting band.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jul-Aug (months 7,8). Cherry-narrowed: the UF/IFAS Broward South Florida planting guide lists cherry tomatoes among June-plantable crops (with okra, southern peas, tropical vegetables) while restricting 'tomatoes (larger fruit varieties)' to Sep-Mar; legacy zone-11 note: new fruit set fails above ~78°F nighttime. Peak fruit-set-failure months are July-August.
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_narrowed: Yes -- same direction as se_gulf (cherry's heat resistance narrows the summer pause), NOT the absolute desert pause. Distinct from se_gulf in that the peninsula has NO frost gap and NO spring crop: it is a single cool-season window with a two-month peak-summer exclusion, not two crops bracketing a one-month pause. Larger-fruited beefsteak will re-derive (wider; likely cool-season-only with a longer exclusion).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11) cherry tomato has no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window: CTAHR states tomato can be "grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted" to the local area. Seed is started indoors in any month and transplanted about 3 to 5 weeks after sowing (CTAHR HGV-5); the plant-level baseline of six weeks indoors is the cooler-mainland figure. The year-round window rests on cultivar choice -- the locally bred, nematode- and disease-resistant UH cultivars (the determinate 'Anahu', 'Healani', 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate hybrids in the N-series) plus cherry types -- rather than on hitting a particular season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
start_indoors.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round'. Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (frost_free_days 365). Resolver keys 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set). Mirrors lettuce hawaii_tropical (m15_na3g), adapted from direct_sow to the transplant (start_indoors + plant_out) shape because tomato is transplanted.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set cherry tomato transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR's home-garden tomato guidance gives a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii contingent on adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer exclusion stated; the limiting factors named are disease, insect, and rain pressure, not a season boundary. Keeping plants caged or staked and off the ground, and irrigating the soil rather than the foliage (in the morning when overhead water is used), are the management levers. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
plant_out.from_year_round_note: Region-constant plant_out uses a distinct from:'year_round' anchor (not a frost anchor overloaded with window_days:365), so the resolver keys 'use authored windows as-is' off a named anchor and resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable. Verifier asserts: region plant_out anchor == 'year_round' <=> resolved-cell year_round flag set.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cherry tomatoes begin ripening about two months after transplant. CTAHR gives most tomato varieties 60 to 80 days to mature; cherry types sit at the fast end, and the crop-level cherry figure is roughly 55 to 70 days (about 62 mid). Because planting is year-round and the UH-bred hybrids are indeterminate -- producing continuously while healthy -- harvest is effectively continuous across the year from successive and overlapping plantings. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: cherry tomato is planted and harvested continuously through the year. Production does not close at a frost or at a sustained-heat date; it is refreshed by successive plantings, which also helps stay ahead of the disease and pest pressure CTAHR flags as the real constraint in Hawaii. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or heat boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for cherry tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Cherry types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.
11.calendar_basis: Cherry tomato is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free, frost_free_days 365) and no summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted to the area, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. This is the per-region source finding: the cherry summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula and the deserts does not universalize to Hawaii's oceanic lowland (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted). Hawaii's challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally-bred cultivars and cultural practice, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); year_round:true makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, cherry tomatoes grow year-round, so you can start a few plants in any month rather than waiting for a season. There is no frost here, so the calendar is open all year. The hard part is not heat but pests and disease, which thrive in the warm, humid weather, plus heavy rain that can crack the fruit. Give yourself the best odds: pick varieties bred for Hawaii or tough cherry types, keep plants up off the ground on a cage or stake, water the soil rather than the leaves (in the morning if you use a sprinkler), and start a fresh planting every few months so you always have healthy young plants coming on. Cherry types and a few compact varieties also do well in 3 to 5 gallon pots.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for cherry tomato: plant and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in the state by choosing locally adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set exclusion. This is the per-region finding, not a default: the cherry summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11) and for the low and high deserts does not carry to Hawaii's oceanic lowland, whose nights do not sustain the fruit-set-stopping highs of peninsular summer. The binding constraints here are disease and pests: tomato spotted wilt virus (thrips-vectored) and tobacco mosaic virus, plus warm-wet fungal and bacterial leaf spots and blights, whitefly, leafminer, and fruit fly, along with fruit cracking in heavy rain. CTAHR's primary lever is genetic: the locally bred, root-knot-nematode- and disease-tolerant UH cultivars, the determinate open-pollinated 'Anahu', 'Healani', and 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate N-series hybrids that fruit continuously while healthy; cherry types and compact determinates such as 'Healani' suit 3 to 5 gallon containers. Cultural practice carries the rest: stake or cage to keep fruit off the ground, irrigate the soil (not the foliage; morning if overhead), and refresh with successive plantings. Most varieties mature in 60 to 80 days, cherry types at the fast end. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5 (Home Garden Tomato), with the 1943 bulletin B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii) as historical corroboration only.

plantings_provenance.shape: region_constant_plantings_plus_resolved_by_zone (year-round/aseasonal; transplant shape -- start_indoors + plant_out, NOT lettuce's direct_sow)
plantings_provenance.succession_carried_by: succession_policy + resolved_by_zone notes (mirrors lettuce hawaii_tropical / northern_tier / fl_peninsula)
plantings_provenance.window_structure: year_round_continuous (Jan-Dec, all 12 months active). CTAHR HGV-5 opens that tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties; cherry tomatoes are named among recommended container types and 'Red Cherry' among cultivars grown in Hawaii. SECOND year-round cell in the dataset (lettuce hawaii_tropical, m15_na3g, was first). NOT the fl_peninsula single-window-with-summer-heat-pause shape and NOT the desert/se_gulf two-window shape: no summer no-sow exclusion for cherry tomato in Hawaii's oceanic lowland.
plantings_provenance.pause_handling: PAUSELESS -- no heat_pause and no cold_pause objects. POSITIVE declaration per the locked treatment: (1) calendar_basis prose reason on resolved_by_zone[11]; (2) year_round:true flag. calendar[] carries NO pause state, so the declare_one_outcome_invariant (Refinement A, all-active scope) REQUIRES year_round:true + calendar_basis -- both present. heat_pause deliberately NOT added: it would encode a no-sow exclusion contradicting the explicit T1 year-round statement (same reasoning as lettuce Decision 1).
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_decision: Cherry summer heat_pause does NOT apply to hawaii_tropical. Per-region source finding, consistent with the standing guardrail (heat_pause read from source per region, never universalized). fl_peninsula carries Jul-Aug because UF/IFAS documents sustained nights above about 78°F stopping fruit set in larger types there; the deserts carry an absolute Jun-Aug. CTAHR makes the OPPOSITE explicit statement for Hawaii (year-round by variety choice) and names disease/pest/rain, not a fruit-set season gap, as the constraint. crops.description_seasoned: Cherry tomatoes are the most forgiving class in the tomato family for first-season growers, for a specific biological reason: most are indeterminate, meaning they continue producing new flower clusters and fruit continuously from first flowering until frost kills the plant. A single healthy plant can yield fruit over 10-14 weeks rather than all at once. The category spans a wide range: round cherries, pear-shaped types, elongated Romas, and cocktail-sized varieties, with fruit sizes from under half an inch to golf-ball. Most modern hybrid cherries (Sun Gold, Sweet 100, Supersweet 100) are also bred for disease tolerance, which further lowers the failure risk. Compact determinate cultivars such as Patio Choice and Tumbling Tom are suited to containers and small-space gardens. In warm climates (zones 9-11), second plantings in late summer can extend harvest into winter. In the coldest growing zones (3-5), short-season varieties (under 60 days to maturity) are the practical choice.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when fully colored, red, yellow, orange, or black depending on variety, and slightly soft to a gentle squeeze. Full color indicates that lycopene synthesis (in red types) or anthocyanin and carotenoid accumulation (in other types) is complete, which correlates with peak sugar content and flavor volatiles. The fruit should detach with a slight twist rather than requiring pulling; resistance to easy separation means the abscission zone has not yet fully formed. The skin losing its sheen is a reliable visual cue: the epidermis transitions from a taut, reflective surface to a slightly matte finish as cell turgor shifts during final ripening. Harvest in the morning when temperatures are cooler, as fruit held at 90°F+ deteriorates faster than fruit harvested and moved to shade.

crops.name: Beefsteak Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Beefsteaks do best in loose, well-draining soil with plenty of organic matter: think compost-rich garden beds rather than hard clay. Good drainage matters a lot: if water pools after rain and takes more than an hour to soak in, the bed needs improvement before planting. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting is the single most useful thing you can do for first-season beefsteaks. Avoid heavy clay soil if possible; if that's what you have, raised beds filled with a mix of topsoil and compost will work much better.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Beefsteak tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter. The plant's indeterminate, heavily fruiting habit places sustained demand on the soil, with large fruit set straining calcium and phosphorus uptake, both of which become restricted in poorly drained or compacted soils. Adequate drainage is non-negotiable: waterlogged roots invite Pythium root rot and close off the aerobic zone that drives nitrogen cycling. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting builds both structure and fertility. Beefsteaks are heavy feeders from fruit set through harvest; organically rich soil reduces the mid-season supplemental fertilizer burden and moderates the calcium-availability swings that drive blossom-end rot.

ph.note_beginner: Beefsteaks want slightly acidic soil: a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. Outside that range, nutrients the plant needs get locked up in the soil even if they're there. Blossom-end rot (the dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit) is often triggered by pH problems limiting how much calcium the plant can absorb. If you've never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit from a garden center is worth doing before your first season. Many extension offices also offer low-cost testing.
ph.note_seasoned: Tomatoes are particularly sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, three nutrients they consume in large quantities. At pH below 5.5, manganese and aluminum become increasingly available at phytotoxic levels; blossom-end rot risk rises as calcium uptake is impaired. Above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation regions, growers routinely need to acidify before planting. Eastern soils often run naturally in the preferred range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.
