start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start beefsteak seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. In the Southeast and Gulf region that is roughly mid-February for the Georgia interior (zone 8) and two to three weeks earlier toward the warmer Gulf-coastal zone 9 end. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: the last week of March or first week or two of April
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set beefsteak transplants out in spring once frost danger passes. UGA gives late March into the first half of April for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs two to three weeks earlier. Beefsteak is large-fruited and slower to mature than cherry types, so time it to set fruit before peak summer heat arrives. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Beefsteak begins ripening roughly three months after transplanting (about 75 to 90 days to maturity, longer than cherry types). The spring crop comes in from late June, just as the summer heat begins to shut fruit set down. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop ends as summer heat sets in. Large-fruited tomatoes are more sensitive to high day and night temperatures than cherry types, so blossom drop and fruit-set failure begin earlier for beefsteak, by about June. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the late-summer transplant date, roughly mid-to-late spring across the region. Because beefsteak needs 75 to 90 days to mature, start early enough that the fall transplant can go out as soon as the summer heat-pause lifts. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant the following vegetables no later than July 20 ... tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out as the worst summer heat eases so plants establish and produce into the cooler fall. UGA gives a fall tomato deadline of about July 20 for middle Georgia (zone 8) so the crop matures before frost; large-fruited beefsteak, being slower than cherry, should hit the early end of the fall window. The warmer zone 9 end runs about two weeks later, into early August. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about three months after the late-summer transplant, bringing beefsteak tomatoes in from roughly October across the region. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Harvest mature green peppers and tomatoes before frost gets them
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to first frost. Large-fruited beefsteak has a shorter productive fall tail here than quick-maturing cherry types. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit-set failure is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Large-fruited beefsteak is more heat-sensitive than cherry types (which are heat resistant), so its summer pause is wider, running across June through August rather than the single midsummer month a cherry holds. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow beefsteak tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Big beefsteak tomatoes handle the heat less well than small cherry tomatoes, so their summer break is longer, running through most of the summer. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the heat, then plant again in late summer once the worst heat passes for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two beefsteak seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Large-fruited beefsteak is more heat-sensitive than cherry types, so its summer pause is wider, spanning roughly June through August rather than a single midsummer month. Beefsteak also needs 75 to 90 days to mature, longer than cherry, so time the spring crop to set fruit before peak heat and set the fall crop out promptly once the heat eases (UGA gives a July 20 fall deadline for middle Georgia so the crop beats frost). The warmer zone 9 end plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UGA Cooperative Extension C943 gives two major planting periods (spring March-May, fall mid-July-September) with an explicit fall tomato deadline (no later than July 20 for middle Georgia), corroborated by UF/IFAS VH021 (North FL tomato Late Mar-Apr + Aug). Two-window is the source grammar, not analogy.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: WIDER than cherry (Jun-Aug vs single Jul). Large-fruited tomatoes are not heat-set-bred and abort flowers at lower thresholds (UF/IFAS VH021: 'Cherry types are heat resistant' -- large-fruited not; Alabama Coop Ext and U.Missouri IPM: day >85 / night >72 deg-F abort). SE/Gulf high summer breaches this June through August.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant beefsteak tomatoes once, in spring (April into May), and the same plant produces all summer into fall. You do not need a second planting. Big beefsteak tomatoes may slow down and set fewer fruit during the hottest weeks of summer, then pick back up as the nights cool in late summer and fall.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow beefsteak as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited beefsteak sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild South Coast you have a long stretch to plant beefsteak tomatoes, from April all the way to mid-July, and you only need to plant once. The coast stays mild enough that there is no hot-summer break. Plant when you like in that window and harvest from summer into late fall.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south) gives beefsteak a long single planting window, April through mid-July, with harvest from summer into late fall. The mild marine climate means there is no hard summer fruit-set pause, so unlike the interior valleys or deserts, beefsteak does not need a heat break here. Choose your planting date within the window to match how you want to pace the harvest. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Table 13.2 (South Coast) gives tomatoes as April-July 15, a single long mild-marine window; San Diego County MG corroborates the long coastal season. Single band, no fall split, no heat_pause (mild marine summer does not breach the set-failure threshold as a hard exclusion).

(UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

Large-fruited beefsteak is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry, so this Jun-Aug pause is not narrowed (it cannot be shortened the way a marginal-zone pause can). (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert (Imperial and Coachella valleys) you grow beefsteak tomatoes in the cool months, not the summer. Plant the main crop from December through March so it makes fruit before the extreme heat, and plant a second crop in early fall (around September) once the worst heat breaks. Summer (June through August) is simply too hot for any tomato to set fruit, so the plants rest then.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow beefsteak on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for beefsteak, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the southern high desert (around Las Cruces, New Mexico) you can grow beefsteak tomatoes in spring and again in fall, with a hot-summer gap. Plant the spring crop in late March or early April so it makes fruit before the July heat. You can try a fall crop planted in mid-July, but big beefsteak tomatoes set fruit poorly in the July and August heat and are slow to ripen, so the fall crop is a bit of a gamble before the November frost. Pick fast-maturing, heat-tolerant varieties.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The southern high desert (Las Cruces, Mesilla Valley; Chihuahuan high desert, zone 8) runs two beefsteak windows split by peak summer heat. Set the spring crop out in late March to early April, after the local last frost (about March 19), so it sets fruit before July. A fall crop can be transplanted in mid-July per the Dona Ana County Master Gardener chart, but for large-fruited beefsteak this is marginal: fruit set is poor once day temperatures exceed 95 °F through July and August, and a 75-90 day plant only just matures before the November frost (about November 12). Favor fast-maturing, heat-tolerant cultivars for the fall attempt. The fall window and two-window structure rest on the single Las Cruces Master Gardener chart, a regional source; the spring dates are anchored to the high-desert frost data with NOAA cross-check. (NMSU Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart)

11.calendar_basis: Beefsteak tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's tropical lowlands you can plant beefsteak tomatoes any month of the year; there is no cold winter and no planting season to wait for. The catch is that big beefsteak tomatoes do not set fruit well in the warm tropical nights, so they do best at cooler elevations and in the cooler parts of the year, and you will have the most luck with heat-tolerant or locally bred varieties. The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical zone 11 grows beefsteak year-round: CTAHR gives a year-round planting capability for most of the islands contingent on adapted varieties, with no winter cold pause and no documented summer no-sow exclusion. The important caveat for beefsteak specifically is fruit-set quality, not timing: CTAHR's field production guidance notes that large-fruited varieties are sensitive to high night temperatures and set fruit poorly in the warm lowland (optimum set 60-70 °F), unlike heat-resistant cherry types. Favor cooler-elevation siting, the cooler part of the year, and heat-tolerant or locally bred wilt-resistant cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, the N-series). The dominant production challenges here are disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant varieties and cultural practice rather than a seasonal stop. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: NONE as a no-sow exclusion (HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). DIVERGES from cherry in PROSE only: CTAHR Field Production Guide flags large-fruited types for poor lowland-night fruit set (optimum 60-70 deg-F) -- disclosed as a quality caveat in region_notes_seasoned, NOT a structural pause. The no-pause structure is the source finding; the size-specific set caveat is the honest beefsteak-vs-cherry difference.

crops.description_seasoned: Indeterminate, large-fruited tomatoes grown for slicing. The beefsteak label covers three biologically close sub-types: true beefsteak-shape varieties (Big Boy, Mortgage Lifter), oblate globe slicers commonly marketed as beefsteak (Celebrity), and large heirloom slicers (Brandywine), with uniform cultivation requirements across all. Indeterminate growth means the plant continues extending and setting fruit until frost kills it; this also means it requires strong caging or staking from the start. Large fruit mass places sustained calcium and water demand on the plant, which is the main reason blossom-end rot and cracking are more common in beefsteaks than in cherry or paste types. Requires a long frost-free window: most varieties need 75-100 days from transplant to first ripe fruit, making them marginal in short-season zones (3-4) without season-extension measures. In zones 9-11, the challenge reverses: summer heat above 90°F causes blossom drop, and fall planting is the standard workaround.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit has reached full variety color all the way to the shoulders, yields to gentle pressure without feeling mushy, and the skin has transitioned from a hard glossy sheen to a softer, slightly matte surface. Skin sheen loss signals the completion of cell-wall softening as lycopene (or variety-appropriate anthocyanins for dark varieties) accumulates and pectin in the outer cell layers begins breaking down. The abscission zone at the stem attachment weakens as the fruit ripens; slight twist resistance is still present at peak eating quality; zero resistance means overripe. Shoulders turning color last: a fruit that is red-sided but green-shouldered is underripe. For large beefsteak fruit (12-16 oz), allow a few extra days compared to cherry or slicer types; mass slows the ripening front.

crops.name: Lettuce (Leaf)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Lettuce likes loose, rich soil that drains well but never dries out completely. Because its roots are shallow and delicate, soggy or packed-down soil hurts lettuce more than it would a tomato, and letting the bed dry out even briefly makes the leaves turn bitter and the plant go to seed early. The simplest fix for almost any soil is to mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the top few inches before you plant, which helps sandy soil hold water and helps heavy soil drain. Try to avoid thick clay, it forms a hard crust that small seedlings struggle to push through and stays wet around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lettuce is widely adaptable on the texture front, and although it produces well in almost any soil that drains freely, a fertile loam or sandy loam that stays high in organic matter and holds moisture well is where it does best. Its root system is shallow and fine, so it is far less forgiving of compaction and waterlogging than deeper-rooted crops, and consistent moisture is essential because even brief drought stress checks vegetative growth and pushes the plant toward bolting. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before sowing improves both drainage on heavier soils and water retention on sandy ones. Heavy clay is the main texture to avoid, it crusts as seedlings emerge and holds water around the roots.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. If your soil is more acidic than 6.0 or more alkaline than 7.0, lettuce can show yellowing leaves or browning edges even when fertilizer is present. The only way to know your number is to test, so get an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office before adding lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it.
ph.note_seasoned: Soil pH governs nutrient availability, and lettuce is most productive in the slightly acidic 6.0 to 6.8 band where phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium stay soluble. Below about 6.0, calcium uptake falls off and aluminum and manganese grow more available, which can scorch leaf margins and stunt the fine root system. Above 7.0, iron and manganese begin to lock up and drive interveinal yellowing on new growth. Across the alkaline interior West and in alkaline-irrigation districts, growers often acidify before planting, while the naturally acidic soils of the forested East more often need lime to reach the target band.

3.notes: Direct sow early. Succession sow every 2 weeks for steady supply. Use cold frame for earliest and latest harvests.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. (MSU Extension) Sow seeds in the spring as soon as the soil is workable. Direct sow when soil consistently reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost in most zones. (UMN Extension)

uscrn_validation.zone_coverage_note_seasoned: station-years 28 below 30 confidence threshold; verdict uses available data but should not be auto-applied

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: For a fall lettuce crop, sow seeds in early to mid July so the crop matures in the cooling temperatures of late summer and fall rather than in midsummer heat, which causes bolting. Use fast-maturing looseleaf varieties so the crop is ready before the first fall frost. (NDSU Extension; UMN Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce can begin harvest 40–60 days after direct sowing under spring conditions, depending on variety and growing conditions; leaf types are at the fast end of this range. Days to maturity for leaf lettuce range from 40 to 80 days depending on the type. (University of Maryland Extension) Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UMN Extension)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall lettuce in cold zones is grown from fast-maturing looseleaf varieties, with the first leaves ready about 45 days after sowing. Cooler fall temperatures slow growth, but harvesting young leaves cut-and-come-again keeps the crop within the short window before frost. (NDSU Extension; University of Maryland Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest spring cool-season crops before sustained heat causes bolting (flowering), which renders leaves bitter and unpalatable. (UMN Extension) Lettuce may bolt and taste bitter when grown in the heat of summer. (UMN Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season greens such as lettuce and spinach tolerate light frost and can often be harvested through the first fall frost. Leaf lettuce may continue growing past the first frost with row cover protection but should be harvested before extended hard freezes. (UMN Extension; Cornell Extension; Iowa State Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Harvest extends to approximately first_frost + 5 days for hardy greens; first_frost - 5 days for tender greens like lettuce.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring succession arm: sow looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks from when soil reaches 40 degrees F through the bolt-driven close of the spring window. Leafy greens germinate at 35-40 degrees F minimum and mature in 40-60 days, so sequential plantings give consistent production; the arm ends as rising heat (above ~75 degrees F) triggers bolting and bitterness. (USU Extension; UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Spring arm capped at the fall-arm start so spring and fall sowings do not overlap in the coldest zones. Latest spring sow otherwise bounded by spring-harvest close minus 30-day baby-leaf maturity (Clause B).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall succession arm: sow fast-maturing looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks starting about 3 months before the first fall frost, harvesting baby leaves as temperatures cool. Lettuce is semi-hardy and tolerates light frost, so the latest sowing leaves roughly 30 days to baby-leaf size near the first frost rather than a full head well before it. Zone 3 fall sow is clamped to the ~July 1 heat floor (first_frost - 76) rather than first_frost - 90, which would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (thermoinhibition above 80 degrees F soil). (UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension; USU Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Fall arm start = heat-floored first_frost offset (methodology v1.5 Clause A). Latest sow = first_frost - 30d (baby-leaf; light-frost-tolerant, no extra hard margin). Per-arm count derived per zone (Clause C); not the season cap.

3.safe_sowing_note_seasoned: Safest sowings: around Apr 29 in spring and Jul 1 for the fall crop. The earliest possible spring date risks slow germination in cold soil, and late-spring sowings run into bolting heat; a mid-spring sowing after the soil has warmed is the most reliable. The first fall sowing, once peak summer heat eases, establishes most dependably.
3.safe_sowing_note_beginner: If you only plant once or twice, aim for about Apr 29 in spring and Jul 1 in late summer. Very early spring is risky because cold soil makes seeds slow to sprout, and late spring gets too hot, making lettuce bitter and causing it to go to seed (bolt).

4.notes: Fast turn-around makes lettuce ideal for succession planting. Heat-tolerant varieties extend season.
