Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion; the warm edge of this cold region carries both a midsummer heat gap and a winter cold pause. (University of Minnesota Extension; Virginia Cooperative Extension)

7.notes: Fall crop is excellent, can harvest through winter in mild Zone 7 with light protection.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Midsummer heat gap (June, July, August): sustained temperatures above roughly 75°F drive lettuce to bolt and turn bitter, and warm soil inhibits germination, so the spring succession ends and no new sowing occurs until the crop resumes as a fall planting. Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion; the warm edge of this cold region carries both a midsummer heat gap and a winter cold pause. (University of Minnesota Extension; Virginia Cooperative Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), lettuce is a spring-and-fall crop built around frost, not heat. Start sowing in spring as soon as the soil warms to about 40°F, usually a few weeks before your last frost, and sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Plant again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. Skip the hottest part of summer, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. For the most reliable results your first season, aim for the spring window from when the soil is workable into early summer, and a fall sowing in July or August depending on your zone, leaving roughly a month before your first frost so young leaves size up while it is still mild. Lettuce takes light frost in stride, so a fall crop can keep going right up to the first hard freeze.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is frost-governed and spring-centric, the standard (non-inverted) lettuce pattern the warm regions invert against. Two succession arms bracket the summer: a spring arm sown from the soil-40°F crossing (a few weeks ahead of last frost) through the bolt-driven close as sustained heat above about 75°F sets in, and a fall arm whose start is heat-floored to roughly July 1 in the coldest zones rather than a flat first-frost-minus-90, since the unclamped offset would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (soil thermoinhibition above about 80°F). The fall arm targets fast-maturing looseleaf at the 30-day baby-leaf end, harvested through light frost rather than to a full head, so the latest viable sow sits about 30 days ahead of first frost with no extra hard margin. Per-arm sowing counts are derived per zone (not a fixed season cap) and range roughly 7 to 10 across zones 3 through 7. Frost is the governing constraint at both ends; summer heat is the interior limit. Spring-sow timing is anchored to MSU (cool-season germination minimum 35 to 40°F) and UMN (direct sow as soil reaches 40°F, 2 to 4 weeks before last frost); the fall arm and heat floor to UMN midsummer-planting guidance and USU (fall lettuce 50 to 75 days before maturity, light frost tolerated to 32°F), with NDSU corroboration for the coldest-zone fall window. In the milder cold zones (6 and 7), a cold frame or row cover extends the harvest several weeks past the outdoor season, with slow winter growth that holds the standing crop rather than expanding it; this is season extension under protection, not part of the default outdoor calendar (VCE and UMN give cold frames and row cover a two-to-four-week spring and fall extension).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf region, fall through spring is the primary lettuce season; summer is excluded by heat. Sow after sustained summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall. UGA gives leaf-lettuce fall planting as approximately September 1 to October 1 for middle Georgia, shifting later toward the warmer (zone 9) Gulf-coastal end of the region. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963) In Florida and the Gulf states, lettuce production runs from late September into spring. (UF/IFAS)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The region's second window is late winter into early spring, before returning heat triggers bolting. UGA gives leaf-lettuce spring planting as approximately January 15 to March 1 for middle Georgia, running earlier at the warmer Gulf-coastal end. The window closes as sustained daytime temperatures climb toward bolting; harvest before then. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the region matures more slowly than spring plantings because cooler temperatures and shorter days slow growth; first cuttings run roughly 60 days from sowing for the fall window. UGA lists 60 to 85 days to maturity for lettuce, with leaf types at the faster end. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring-window leaf lettuce begins harvest sooner than the fall window as warming lengthens growth; leaf types reach cut-and-come-again size at the fast end of the maturity range. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; University of Maryland Extension) Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UMN Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The region's harvest closes when returning spring heat triggers bolting, which turns leaves bitter and pushes a seed stalk. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not prolonged heat. (UMN Extension; UGA Cooperative Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: soil and air above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. (UGA Cooperative Extension; UF/IFAS)
Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: soil and air above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. (UGA Cooperative Extension; UF/IFAS)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf region, lettuce is a fall-through-spring crop, the reverse of the North. Plant after summer heat eases (around September), grow it through the mild winter, and plant again in late winter for a spring crop. Skip high summer, when lettuce turns bitter and bolts. Winter is the best, most reliable season here.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted: two cool-season windows (fall sowing from late summer once heat subsides; late-winter sowing before spring heat returns) bracketing a summer heat pause. Peak production is winter (UF/IFAS: highest production January-February). Frost is a secondary modifier at the cooler zone-8 interior end, where hard freezes can damage an exposed crop; lettuce tolerates light frost. Zone-9 Gulf-coastal end runs the windows earlier in spring and later in fall. Windows verified against UGA B577/C963 (leaf lettuce: spring Jan 15-Mar 1, fall Sep 1-Oct 1, middle-Georgia baseline) with UF/IFAS corroboration for the Gulf-coastal end.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar valleys), lettuce has a late-summer/early-fall window as peak summer heat begins to ease. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the Interior Valleys as August, then again November through March. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Sacramento County Master Gardeners note lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil because heat can cause seed dormancy, and bolts under high-temperature stress. (UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The interior's main window is the mild winter into early spring (Table 13.2: November through March), a long cool-season window that opens after the first heat break and closes as returning spring heat triggers bolting. Harvest before sustained spring warmth. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Winter-spring window anchored to the spring bolt close, working back across the Nov-Mar span; mild interior winters keep the window open throughout.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Late-summer-sown leaf lettuce in the interior reaches cut size in roughly 45 days under warm early-fall conditions; leaf types are at the fast end of the maturity range. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Winter-sown leaf lettuce matures over roughly 50 to 60 days as cooler temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to the late-summer window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The interior lettuce season closes as returning spring heat drives bolting, turning leaves bitter and pushing a seed stalk. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. Sacramento County trials saw lettuce bolt during weeks of 106-107 degrees F. (UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County; UC ANR Master Gardener Program)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through July is excluded by interior-valley summer heat: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil (heat-induced seed dormancy) and bolts under high-temperature stress. Sacramento County trials saw bolting in weeks of 106-107°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

May through July is excluded by interior-valley summer heat: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil (heat-induced seed dormancy) and bolts under high-temperature stress. Sacramento County trials saw bolting in weeks of 106-107°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and nearby), lettuce grows in two stretches: a quick late-summer planting in August as the worst heat starts to ease, and a long main season from November through March over the mild winter. Skip the heart of summer (roughly May through July), when it is too hot, lettuce won't germinate well, and plants bolt and turn bitter. Harvest the winter crop before spring heat returns.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior-valley calendar is heat-inverted with two windows (Table 13.2: August, then November through March). The August window is a short late-summer sowing as peak heat eases; the November-March window is the long mild-winter main season, closing as spring heat returns and drives bolting. Summer (roughly May through July) is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil and bolts under high-temperature stress (Sacramento County trials bolted in weeks of 106-107°F). Frost is a minor secondary factor at the cooler zone-8 end. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County corroboration for interior-valley heat behavior.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the California north coast and northern coastal interior (Monterey County north), lettuce is sown from late winter through summer; the cool, foggy maritime summer is the active growing season rather than an exclusion. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the North and North Coast as February through August. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Sow in late winter once the soil is workable and warming. The cold, wet winter, not summer heat, bounds the season here.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce on the cool north coast reaches cut size in roughly 45 to 60 days; leaf types are at the fast end of the maturity range. The mild maritime summer keeps the crop productive across the season. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The north-coast lettuce season runs through summer and closes as the cool, wet winter sets in. Lettuce tolerates light frost but is bounded by the cold, damp end of the year rather than by summer heat. Harvest before extended cold and wet weather. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Cool-limited region: season bounded by the cold/wet winter end (first_frost - 5), not by a spring bolt close. Summer is the active growing season.

9.calendar_basis: Summer is the ACTIVE growing season on the cool maritime north coast; there is no summer heat_pause. The season is bounded at the cold/wet winter end instead (cold_pause in the winter months). Absence of heat_pause is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field).

10.calendar_basis: Summer is the ACTIVE growing season on the cool maritime north coast; there is no summer heat_pause. The season is bounded at the cold/wet winter end instead (cold_pause in the winter months). Absence of heat_pause is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field).

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the California north coast (Monterey County north), summer is actually lettuce's best season, the opposite of hot inland areas. The cool, foggy summers let you grow lettuce from late winter all the way through summer. Plant from February through August. The cold, wet winter, not summer heat, is what ends the season here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: North-coast calendar is cool-limited and summer-inclusive (Table 13.2: February through August), the inverse of the heat-inverted interior and desert. The cool maritime summer is the active growing season, so there is no summer heat pause; the season is bounded instead by the cold, wet winter. Spring sowing begins once soil is workable and warming; the crop runs through summer and closes as winter sets in. In the mildest coastal microclimates, lettuce can be grown nearly year-round with careful variety selection (UC Marin Master Gardeners), but that is a microclimate refinement, not the regional window. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Marin Master Gardeners corroboration for the maritime cool-season pattern.
ca_north_coast.microclimate_note_seasoned: UC Marin Master Gardeners note that lettuce, generally a cool-season annual, can be grown throughout the year in Marin with advance planning and judicious plant selection. This is a maritime microclimate observation dependent on variety choice, carried here as a refinement; the regional window of record is Table 13.2's February through August. (UC Marin Master Gardeners)

bolting.text_beginner: On the cool north coast, summer is your main lettuce season, not something to avoid. Bolting is less of a constant threat here, but it still happens, often as days lengthen in late spring or during an occasional warm spell. When you see a flower stalk shoot up from the center, harvest the whole plant right away; the leaves stay edible but turn more bitter each day.
bolting.text_seasoned: North-coast summers are mild enough that lettuce runs through them; bolting is driven more by lengthening days and occasional heat spells than by a seasonal heat ramp. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Unlike inland regions, you do not pause through summer here.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the California south coast (San Luis Obispo County south), lettuce grows across a long, mild cool season. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the South Coast as August through April. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) The window opens as summer heat eases and runs through the mild winter; San Luis Obispo County Master Gardeners list lettuce among cool-season crops that produce well in the cooler months, with a typical South County last frost around mid-February. (UC Master Gardeners of San Luis Obispo County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce on the mild south coast reaches cut size in roughly 45 to 60 days depending on the season within the window; leaf types are at the fast end. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The south-coast lettuce season closes as returning spring and summer heat drives bolting. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. The mild maritime winter rarely limits the crop; heat is the governing constraint. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through July is a summer gap on the south coast: lettuce bolts and germinates poorly as temperatures rise. The gap is softer than in the interior or desert (the maritime-influenced south coast stays milder) but still falls outside the Table 13.2 sowing window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

May through July is a summer gap on the south coast: lettuce bolts and germinates poorly as temperatures rise. The gap is softer than in the interior or desert (the maritime-influenced south coast stays milder) but still falls outside the Table 13.2 sowing window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the California south coast (San Luis Obispo south), lettuce grows across a long, mild cool season from August all the way through April. The winter is gentle enough that you can keep planting through it. Skip the warmest months (roughly May through July), when lettuce bolts and turns bitter. Harvest the spring plantings before summer heat sets in.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: South-coast calendar is summer-excluded and winter-dominant (Table 13.2: August through April), a single long mild-season window. It opens as summer heat eases and closes as returning heat drives bolting. The summer gap (roughly May through July) is softer here than in the interior or desert because the maritime-influenced coast stays milder, but it still falls outside the sowing window. Frost is essentially not a limiting factor (South County last frost around mid-February per SLO County MG); heat governs both ends. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Master Gardeners of San Luis Obispo County corroboration for the mild south-coast cool season.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the California low desert (Imperial and Coachella Valleys), lettuce is a fall-through-winter crop; summer is excluded entirely by extreme heat. Sow once summer heat subsides in early fall. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the Desert Valleys as September through December. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Imperial County summers run hot and dry (often 90-120 degrees F) with mild winters, and leaf lettuce is a major cool-season crop there. (UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the desert matures over roughly 45 to 60 days; cooler winter temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to warm-season conditions. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The desert lettuce season closes as the spring heat ramp returns; lettuce bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures climb. Harvest before sustained spring heat. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: April through August is excluded by extreme desert heat: soil and air well above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

April through August is excluded by extreme desert heat: soil and air well above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California low desert (Imperial and Coachella Valleys), lettuce is a winter crop. Plant from September through December, grow it through the mild winter, and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. Once spring warms up and days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the heat arrives.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: Desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single fall-through-winter window (Table 13.2: September through December sowing). Summer (roughly April through August) is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap; Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting. Frost is not the limiting factor here. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Cooperative Extension Imperial County corroboration for the low-desert climate.

bolting.text_beginner: In the low desert, lettuce is a winter crop, so grow it from September through December and skip summer entirely. As spring warms and days lengthen, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter fast. When you spot a flower stalk, harvest the whole plant right away, and do not try to carry a crop into the desert summer.
bolting.text_seasoned: Desert lettuce finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp; expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest (southern New Mexico, West Texas), fall is a primary lettuce season: sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf-lettuce fall planting for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) as approximately September 1. The El Paso County planting calendar places leaf lettuce in the fall garden as the heat breaks. (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension EHT-056; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The arid Southwest's second window is late winter into early spring, before lengthening days and returning heat trigger bolting. NMSU notes lettuce germinates best near 65-70F and bolts when temperatures climb above about 70F with long days; the El Paso County calendar plants leaf lettuce as one of the very earliest spring crops. Sow as soon as the soil is workable and harvest before sustained spring heat. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the arid Southwest matures somewhat more slowly than spring plantings as days shorten and cool. NMSU Circular 457-B gives leaf lettuce about 46 days to harvest under favorable conditions; first cuttings of a fall sowing run roughly 50 days. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457-B)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring leaf lettuce reaches first harvest in roughly 46 days from sowing under the lengthening-day conditions of the arid spring. NMSU Circular 457-B gives leaf lettuce about 46 average days to harvest. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457-B)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest closes as returning spring heat and long days trigger bolting, which turns leaves bitter. NMSU: temperatures above about 70F with long days cause lettuce to bolt, and high temperatures cause bitterness. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

8.zone_notes: Arid USDA zone 8 (e.g. Las Cruces NM, El Paso TX): frost-free roughly April through early November. Lettuce runs a spring window (late winter into early spring) and a fall window (late summer into fall), with a hard summer heat pause between them. Light frost is tolerated at the cool winter shoulders; intense summer heat, not frost, governs the season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in the arid Southwest, soil and air above the bolting/germination threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce through the May-August heat. NMSU: lettuce bolts above about 70°F with long days and germination is inhibited above about 79°F. (New Mexico State University Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm arid Southwest, lettuce grows in the cooler shoulders of the year, not the summer. Plant a spring crop in late winter to early spring, and a fall crop in late summer once the worst heat breaks. Skip planting through the summer heat, about May through August, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. If you are squeezing in a last spring sowing, get it in by early May; for fall, wait until the heat eases, usually around late August. Light frost in winter is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted with two cool-season windows bracketing a summer heat pause: a spring window (sow as soil becomes workable in late winter/early spring, harvest before the spring heat ramp triggers bolting) and a fall window (sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer, into fall). The governing constraint is heat, not frost. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf lettuce for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) a fall planting near September 1; the El Paso County calendar runs leaf lettuce as a very-early spring crop and again in fall. NMSU gives leaf lettuce about 46 days to harvest, optimal germination near 65-70°F, and bolting above about 70°F with long days. Frost is a secondary modifier at the cool winter shoulders (arid zone 8 is frost-free roughly April through early November); light frost is tolerated. The summer heat pause (May-August) is a hard exclusion. Windows verified against Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-056 and the El Paso County planting calendar, with NMSU Circular 457/457-B for maturity and bolting biology.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert (Maricopa County ~9b, Yuma), lettuce is a fall-through-winter crop on a single long window; summer is excluded entirely by extreme heat. Sow once summer heat subsides in early-to-mid fall and the soil cools, then continue sowing through the mild winter into late winter. University of Arizona guidance places leaf-lettuce planting across the cool season, and the Yuma calendar gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce and other non-fruiting greens. Plant after about September 15 once nights and soil cool; avoid sowing while soil is at or above 85 degrees F. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005; AZ1615)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the low desert matures over roughly 45 to 65 days; cooler winter temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to warm-season conditions. University of Arizona gives leaf lettuce about 30 to 90 days to harvest depending on variety and season. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach usable size. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The low-desert lettuce season closes as the spring heat ramp returns; lettuce bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures climb. University of Arizona notes germination is inhibited at high temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95 degrees F) and the warm season from March onward suits fruiting crops rather than lettuce. Harvest before sustained spring heat; do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

9.zone_notes: Arizona low desert (USDA zone 9b; Maricopa County/Phoenix, Yuma). Frost is occasional and light; lettuce tolerates the rare light frost but not sustained heat. Last spring frost averages around February 15, but winter is mild growing weather for lettuce rather than a pause. The limiting factor is summer heat, not frost: triple-digit highs return in May and persist through August.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through August is excluded by extreme low-desert heat: soil and air well above the lettuce thermoinhibition range cause germination failure and bolting. In metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May, and June through August average highs of about 104 to 106°F, far above the 77 to 95°F range that inhibits lettuce germination (University of Arizona AZ1099). April (average high about 85°F) is the spring bolting-close for an established crop rather than a no-sow month, and September is the soil-gated fall sow-resume, so the hard no-activity gap is May through August. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma), lettuce is a winter crop. Plant from about mid-September, once nights cool and the soil is no longer hot, and keep sowing through the mild winter into February. Grow it through the winter and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. As spring warms up and the days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the real heat arrives, usually by April. A rare light winter frost is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Low-desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single long fall-through-winter window (sow from about mid-September, once soil drops below the high-temperature germination block, continuing through the mild winter into late February). Summer (May through August) is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. University of Arizona gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce in the low desert; the Yuma calendar names lettuce as a primary cool-season crop over that span, and Maricopa County guidance runs leaf lettuce across the cool months with a summer break. Germination is inhibited at high soil temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95°F), which is why the fall sowing waits for the soil to cool rather than for a frost date. The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting; in metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May. Frost is a minor, occasional modifier at the winter shoulders, not the season boundary. Windows verified against University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005 (Maricopa County), AZ1615 (Yuma), and AZ1099 (lettuce germination physiology).

plantings_provenance.window_structure: single_continuous (Sep-Feb) -- low desert AZ is one long fall-through-winter window per U of A (AZ1615 Sep-Feb cool season; AZ1005 Maricopa leaf-lettuce cool-season run), structurally mirroring fl_peninsula's single window, NOT the two-window warm_arid/se_gulf shape and NOT ca_desert's shorter Sep-Dec window. Decision D2 (Trevor, 2026-06-01): data-driven, not a fl_peninsula analogy borrow -- independently lands on [5,6,7,8] for a sourced desert reason; narrower than ca_desert's [4,5,6,7,8] because the Phoenix April-85F boundary is citable where the Imperial Valley basis did not pin April.

Decision D3 (Trevor, 2026-06-01). Consistent with n=1 (resolver-mechanics rationale, not a manufactured second action-fork).

bolting.text_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, lettuce is a winter crop, so grow it from about mid-September through February and skip summer entirely. As spring warms and the days lengthen, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter fast. When you spot a flower stalk, harvest the whole plant right away, and do not try to carry a crop into the desert summer.
bolting.text_seasoned: Low-desert lettuce finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp; expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb past the mid-80s toward the first 100°F days of early May. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In peninsular Florida (central and south), leaf lettuce is a cool-season crop grown on a single continuous window from fall through late winter. UF/IFAS gives the peninsular planting window as September through February for both central and south Florida. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Sowing begins once the worst summer heat eases in September and continues through February; the regional calendars list lettuce among the crops to plant from October onward, with February the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest in the deep south. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce reaches harvest roughly 60 days after sowing under peninsular Florida's cool-season conditions; UF/IFAS lists lettuce at 60-80 days to harvest. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Fall and early-winter sowings mature into the winter production peak.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular harvest closes in spring as sustained heat returns and triggers bolting, which turns leaves bitter. The last February sowings finish by roughly April; lettuce is absent from the regional plant calendars from March onward as warm-season crops take over. Harvest before sustained daytime heat. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

10.zone_notes: Central Florida (USDA 10 portion, between State Roads 40 and 70). Frost and light freezes are likely in January and February; protect an exposed crop when a freeze is forecast. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: peninsular Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, causing germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Lettuce is absent from the central Florida plant calendar from March onward as warm-season crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

11.zone_notes: South Florida (USDA 11, below State Road 70). Frost and freezes are rare; the limiting factor is summer heat, not cold. February is the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: south Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, ending cool-season production. Lettuce is absent from the south Florida plant calendar from March onward as tropical and heat-tolerant crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, lettuce is a cool-season crop, the opposite of up north. Plant from fall through late winter (about September into February), grow it through the mild winter, and skip the summer, when lettuce turns bitter and goes to seed. Winter is your reliable lettuce season here. For the easiest results, aim for the heart of the season, roughly November through January, when temperatures are most consistently cool, rather than the warm edges in early fall or the spring heat ramp.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted and single-window: one continuous cool-season sowing window (September through February per UF/IFAS VH021 Table 1, central and south Florida) bracketed by a summer heat exclusion, not split into two windows the way the more northern Southeast/Gulf zones are. Peak production is winter. The limiting factor is heat-driven bolting, not frost. The two peninsular zones differ mainly in frost exposure: central Florida (zone 10) sees likely January-February freezes that can damage an exposed crop (cover when a freeze is forecast), while south Florida (zone 11) rarely freezes and is heat-limited at both ends. Windows verified against UF/IFAS VH021 (Table 1) with the central (ENH1189) and south (ENH1191) Florida gardening calendars confirming the March warm-crop flip and the September reopening.

plantings_provenance.window_structure: single_continuous (not two-window) -- peninsular FL is one Sept-Feb window per VH021 Table 1, unlike se_gulf's two-window UGA structure

The plant_out window in plantings[] is authoritative for sowing dates.
plantings_provenance.zone_differentiation_note: z10 (central) and z11 (south) share the Sept-Feb window and the May-Aug heat pause; they differ in frost exposure only (z10 freeze-risk shoulders vs z11 rare frost), encoded in zone_notes + region_notes_seasoned, not in heat_pause months.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11), leaf lettuce is sown year-round; there is no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for the leaf type. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and states that leafy and semi-head types can be grown year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinkler irrigation, and that lettuce is grown year-round in most home and community gardens. Heading types are the seasonal exception (cooler months at low elevation, or high elevation) and are not the leaf-lettuce case here. Sow in any month; the heat of summer is managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade rather than by skipping a season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
direct_sow.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round' (Decision 3, NA-3g). Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (zone_frost_data: frost_free_days 365). The resolver keys its 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' path off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable from it (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce in Hawaii reaches cut size in roughly 50 to 60 days from a direct-seeded sowing; CTAHR gives about 50 to 60 days to harvest for direct-seeded Manoa lettuce, the standard low-elevation leaf type, and a few days earlier from transplants. Harvest single leaves or the whole young head as soon as it reaches usable size; harvesting earlier also sidesteps tip-burn and bolting in warm weather. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: leaf lettuce is sown and harvested continuously through the year. Successive sowings keep a supply coming rather than the crop closing at a frost or a sustained-heat date. In the hottest, longest-day stretch, growth quality dips (tip-burn, faster bolting) but production does not stop; it is managed with cultivar choice and shade. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or bolt boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for leaf lettuce. The limiting factor is summer heat quality, not a season boundary: in the hottest months leaf lettuce is grown with a heat-tolerant cultivar (Manoa, Anuenue) and afternoon shade, or moved to higher elevation, rather than paused. Heavy rain can bruise the soft leaves and is the other warm-month management concern.
11.calendar_basis: Leaf lettuce is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no summer no-sow exclusion: University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation, and states leafy/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations and in most home gardens. The summer heat brings a quality dip (tip-burn, faster bolting), managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade or higher elevation, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); the year_round:true flag makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, leaf lettuce grows year-round, so you can plant a little any month of the year. Pick a heat-tolerant variety such as Manoa or Anuenue, which were bred here to handle the warmth and are slow to bolt. In the hottest, sunniest months, give plants some afternoon shade and keep them well watered, and protect the soft leaves from pounding rain. Lettuce can still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) in a hot spell, so harvest leaves young and often. True head lettuce only does well up at higher, cooler elevations; down near the coast, stick with leaf and semi-head types.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: sow and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and notes that leafy and semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinklers, while heading types are the seasonal, higher-elevation exception. The locally bred 'UH Manoa' (a Green Mignonette selection) and 'Anuenue' are the low-elevation standards; CTAHR describes Manoa as heat-tolerant, slow to bolt, and tip-burn resistant, grown year-round. The hot, long-day months bring a quality dip rather than a production gap: expect faster bolting and more tip-burn, managed with cultivar choice, roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites (per CTAHR shade trials), and a move to higher elevation for head types. Germination falls off above about 81°F, so warm-season sowings benefit from primed seed or a cooler germination spot. Keep soil moisture steady; protect soft-leaved types from heavy rain. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164 (Lettuce Production Guidelines for Hawaii), HGV-2 (Lettuce for the Home Garden), and B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii).

plantings_provenance.succession_carried_by: succession_policy + resolved_by_zone notes (mirrors northern_tier / fl_peninsula / low_desert_az)
plantings_provenance.window_structure: year_round_continuous (Jan-Dec, all 12 months active) -- NEW SHAPE. UH CTAHR RES-164 Table 1 lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation; RES-164 text and HGV-2 confirm leaf/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevation and in home gardens. This is NOT the fl_peninsula/low_desert_az single-window-with-summer-heat-pause shape and NOT the two-window warm_arid/se_gulf shape: there is no summer no-sow exclusion for the leaf type. Decision 1 (Trevor, 2026-06-01, confirmed pauseless): the hot-season quality dip (tip-burn, bolting) is managed with cultivar + shade, not a heat_pause; a heat_pause would encode a no-sow exclusion that directly contradicts the explicit T1 year-round statement. The leaf-vs-head split makes this clean -- the source names this exact type (leaf) as year-round while head types are seasonal.
plantings_provenance.pause_handling: PAUSELESS -- no heat_pause and no cold_pause. Encoded as a POSITIVE declaration per the locked treatment: (1) calendar_basis prose reason on resolved_by_zone[11] (both pauses intentionally absent, CTAHR/elevation/cultivar basis), matching the ca_north_coast no-heat_pause precedent; (2) NET-NEW year_round:true flag on the resolved cell (ca_north_coast still carries detectable cold_pause STATES; Hawaii is the first cell with NO pause signal in calendar[] at all, so the flag makes intent machine-readable). Decision 1 + Refinement A (Trevor, 2026-06-01).

Resolver implication: a year_round cell's windows are frost-independent, so the resolver must NOT frost-offset them -- it uses the authored windows as-is, keyed off direct_sow from:'year_round' and/or this flag.
plantings_provenance.declare_one_outcome_invariant: Refinement A (Trevor, 2026-06-01): SCOPED TO THE ALL-ACTIVE CASE. A resolved cell whose calendar[] contains NO pause state (no heat_pause/cold_pause/season_over) MUST carry year_round:true plus its calendar_basis reason. A cell with any pause state in calendar[] is self-declaring and passes without a flag or pause object (passes ca_north_coast: cold_pause STATES + prose, no object; passes future northern_tier). Refinement B: this invariant is SEPARATE from the calendar-model spec Section 6 calendar<->pause-object sync invariant -- Section 6 catches 'calendar disagrees with the pause object it has' (needs an object); this new one catches 'pause entirely omitted, cell silently reads all-active'. Both run; neither absorbs the other.

Crop-level days_to_maturity [30,45] is the mainland baby/looseleaf figure; the Hawaii cell uses the CTAHR Manoa figure, mirroring how low_desert_az used the AZ-local maturity rather than the crop-level value.

This is the genuine fork the kickoff flagged Hawaii as the most likely cell to surface (n=1 discipline: authored on evidence of real action divergence, not manufactured). bolting.text_beginner: In Hawaii you grow lettuce year-round, so you do not skip a season; instead you manage the heat. Use a heat-tolerant variety like Manoa or Anuenue, give plants afternoon shade in the hottest, brightest months, and keep them watered. They will still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) faster in a warm spell, so harvest leaves young and pick the whole plant once you see a stalk. Up at cooler, higher elevations, bolting is slower and you have more leeway.
bolting.text_seasoned: Hawaii is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: manage bolting with cultivar and microclimate rather than a seasonal pause. Grow heat-tolerant types (UH Manoa, Anuenue), add roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites, and harvest young; bolting and tip-burn accelerate with heat and long days. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Higher elevations extend the bolt-free window; head types are reliable only up there.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the fastest, most forgiving crops in the garden, and a strong first-season choice. Sow it directly where it will grow and harvest the outer leaves as cut-and-come-again, taking the oldest first while the center keeps producing. Lettuce is a cool-season crop: it bolts and turns bitter once sustained heat arrives, so the productive window is the cool shoulders of the year. Succession sow small batches every couple of weeks through spring, then again in fall, to keep tender leaves coming rather than harvesting one bed all at once.
crops.description_beginner: One of the fastest and most forgiving crops you can grow, and a great pick for a first garden. Sow the seed right where the plants will grow, then harvest the outer leaves a few at a time, taking the oldest first while the center keeps making new ones. Lettuce is a cool-season crop, which means it grows best in the mild parts of the year: once steady heat arrives it turns bitter and sends up a flower stalk (this is called bolting). To keep tender leaves coming, sow a small batch every couple of weeks in spring, then again in fall, instead of planting one big bed all at once.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick the outer leaves whenever they reach usable size, taking the oldest from several plants and leaving the crown to keep growing, or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the crown for a single larger harvest that regrows. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when leaves are crisp and full of water. The limiting factor is heat: once the central stem begins to elongate (bolting), the plant shifts to flowering, and the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your fullest harvests before sustained warm weather sets in.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick the outer leaves whenever they are big enough to use, taking the oldest ones from several plants and leaving the center to keep growing. Or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the base for one larger harvest that will grow back. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when the leaves are crisp and full of water. Heat is the limiting factor: once a stalk starts to rise from the center (this is bolting, the plant shifting to making flowers), the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your biggest harvests before steady warm weather arrives.

versioning_note: Two version fields. `version` tracks crop content (planting dates, sources, biological data) and bumps when data inside `crops` changes. `schema_version` tracks the shape of the dataset (rule structure, sub-object schemas, top-level fields) and bumps when structure changes. They are independent. As of schema_version 2.8, deployed structure includes: symmetric `_seasoned`/`_beginner` register suffixing on prose fields (Phase 0); the three-array companions register-by-membership model (`*_beginner`/`*_beginner_seasoned`/`*_seasoned`); the additive `regions{}` sibling with `northern_tier` lifted and warm regions scaffolded PENDING (Phase A/B); and the calendar-model scaffolding (session 4c): a `track` field (`beginner`/`succession`/`second_planting`) on each `plantings[]` entry, a crop-level `calendar_basis` (`frost_anchored`/`non_seasonal_indoor`/`generic_placeholder`) with the relaxed validator `plantings` length >= 1 UNLESS `calendar_basis` explains it, and the extended `calendar[]` vocabulary adding `cold_pause`/`heat_pause`/`season_over` (reserved; populated per-crop in gold-standard arcs, not bulk-applied).

uscrn.name: NOAA U.S. Climate Reference Network (USCRN)
uscrn.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information / Atmospheric Turbulence and Diffusion Division
uscrn.note: Network-level reference: Diamond, H.J., T.R. Karl, M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, J.E. Bell, R.D. Leeper, D.R. Easterling, J.H. Lawrimore, T.P. Meyers, M.R. Helfert, G. Goodge, and P.W. Thorne, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network after One Decade of Operations: Status and Assessment. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 94(4), 485-498. DOI: 10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00170.1. Soil moisture and temperature methodology reference: Bell, J.E., M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, W.G. Collins, J.H. Lawrimore, R.D. Leeper, M.E. Hall, J. Kochendorfer, T.P. Meyers, T. Wilson, and H.J. Diamond, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture and Temperature Observations. J. Hydrometeor., 14(3), 977-988. DOI: 10.1175/JHM-D-12-0146.1. Triplicate-redundancy variability companion: Palecki, M.A., and J.E. Bell, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture Observations with Triple Redundancy: Measurement Variability. Vadose Zone J., 12(2), vzj2012.0158. DOI: 10.2136/vzj2012.0158. USCRN provides the soil-temperature observations used to validate this dataset's soil-temp planting anchors at zone level. Soil moisture and temperature are measured in triplicate at five depths (5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 cm); anchors in this dataset are validated against the 5 cm depth record.
uscrn.citable_for: NOAA US Climate Reference Network station-level climate data. Citable for soil-temperature, air-temperature, and precipitation observational data feeding the Phase 1.1 anchor pipeline. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims.

weatherkit.name: Apple WeatherKit
weatherkit.note: WeatherKit is the resolution-layer data source for bolt-threshold and heat-pause anchors. Underlying service: Apple Weather. Data products used: current conditions, hourly forecast (10-day, up to 240 hours), and daily forecast (10 days). Coverage: global, with US coordinate-level resolution adequate for gardener microclimate purposes; updates hourly to sub-hourly. WeatherKit is a forecast service, not a historical-validation dataset; its role in this dataset is resolution at notification time, not validation. Known limitation: 10-day forecast horizon constrains sustain-window math for bolt thresholds in cool-season crops where the relevant window can exceed 10 days; the methodology page documents the resolution approach for that case. Per Apple's WeatherKit attribution requirements, apps that display Apple Weather data must include the Apple Weather trademark and a link to additional data sources.
weatherkit.citable_for: Apple WeatherKit API for weather forecast and current-conditions data. Citable for forecast-driven app behavior. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims; not a research source.

previous_remediations.summary: Phase 1.1 v2.2 dataset integration. Attached uscrn_validation sub-objects to 414 soil-temp-anchored rules using Session 7's validator verdicts, and resolution_source sub-objects to 480 bolt-threshold and heat-pause-anchored rules pointing to WeatherKit. Per-zone source citations on uscrn_validation derived from launch_anchors.json zone_attributions. The resolution_source.anchor_threshold field carries the rule's `from` enum verbatim (e.g., bolt_threshold_start); actual temperature threshold is resolved app-side at runtime via WeatherKit. fallback_beyond_horizon set to stored_date with UI signaling planned app-side.

No changes to crops, source_catalog, zone_frost_data, zone_sources, or rule-level fields. Architecture doc bumped to v2.3 in parallel; methodology page draft (`methodology_page_draft.md`) produced as the main Session 10 deliverable.
